title: Defence lawyer in Cornell University case calls for special prosecutor Letitia James to be removed
description: A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recu
body: A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recuse herself over past public comments.The lawyer had said a social media post from New York Attorney General Letitia James throws into question her investigation's "integrity and independence".In the 28 September post, James wrote that "what this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable" and told survivors that "we stand with you".The university's administration is under fire over its alleged mishandling of the October 2024 incident and, according to US media, now faces a no-confidence vote by Cornell faculty. The university's Faculty Senate, a governing body comprised of professors and other academic staff, will vote on a resolution of no confidence next week, according to reports.  Cornell is an Ivy League university, alongside Harvard and Yale, and its faculty includes Nobel laureates and other distinguished researchers.A majority no-confidence vote would be a largely symbolic gesture, signalling the broader faculty's discontent and applying pressure on university leadership to act.Cornell University announced on Tuesday that it was hiring Sally Yates, a former deputy attorney general, to lead an independent review of the university's practices and procedures on sexual assault and related conduct."Yates and her team will conduct a detailed review of the University's response to the allegations involving Jane Doe", the university said in a statement, "including whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to the matter".Allegations made in a lawsuit against seven men and the university have rocked the campus in New York state, with hundreds of students and faculty members gathering there on Monday in protest, and sparked anger across the country.New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week appointed James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case and how law enforcement and the university initially responded to the allegations made by a woman identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe.Jane Doe has accused the university of failing to protect her, after she was allegedly drugged and raped by the men for several hours at a fraternity party. Days before she was appointed special prosecutor, James wrote on X: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. "I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers," she continued. "To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."The lawyer for one of the seven accused said these remarks were disqualifying. In a statement sent to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the lawyer said her comments conflict with the need for "independently evaluating the evidence"."This is not an accusation that Attorney General James is corrupt, acting in bad faith or incapable of performing her duties professionally," the statement said. "Nor am I suggesting that a court has determined that she is legally disqualified. The point is much narrower: an avoidable question now hangs over this investigation, and voluntary recusal would remove it."Governor Hochul and James were questioned about impartiality concerns during a news conference, and Hochul said James would "follow the facts". "She'll examine the evidence and go wherever it leads, and if the evidence supports charges, she will pursue them," Hochul said.

schema.headline: Defence lawyer in Cornell University case calls for special prosecutor Letitia James to be removed

title: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centres
description: Finnish authorities have ordered a halt to building work at two planned Google data centres amid concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares
body: Finnish authorities have ordered a halt to building work at two planned Google data centres amid concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.The sites form part of Google's record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago and described by the company as its largest single investment in Europe.The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) said work at one site was carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment and ordered measures that would "significantly alter the environment" to be suspended by 23 October.Google said it had "fallen short of our own high standards in this instance" and would follow the agency's guidance.The orders relate to preparatory work carried out at the planned data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani.According to LVV's head of environment Tommi Muilu, work at the sites included the removal of trees and topsoil, the construction of site roads and storage areas, and changes to ditches.Tuike Finland, the company behind Google's data centre projects, has been asked to provide an explanation and set out how it intends to proceed by 14 October. The agency said it could begin "enforcement proceedings" if the company failed to comply with its demand.Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, had previously told the AFP news agency that "nature sites which should be preserved" had been felled. The conservation group had previously called for work to be halted while the environmental requirements were examined.In a statement to the BBC, Google said: "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance."It said it had "acted in good faith under the Forestry Act", carried out nature surveys and put measures in place to protect areas of high environmental value."As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos," the company added.Google announced last month that it would invest at least €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) in Finland over 2027 and 2028. Its plans included new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, alongside investment in its existing facility in Hamina.The company said the infrastructure would help it meet growing demand for services including Search, Maps and its AI assistant Gemini.Google said the construction phase in 2027 and 2028 would support more than 37,000 jobs and contribute an average of €3.6bn a year to Finland's economy.As part of its expansion, Google also signed a 22-year power purchasing agreement with Finnish energy company Fortum covering up to half the capacity of the Loviisa nuclear power plant. Fortum said the agreement would help support the plant's continued operation until 2050.Finland has attracted growing interest in data centres, with its cool climate and low-carbon electricity among the factors making it attractive to developers. Lower temperatures can also reduce the energy required to cool facilities filled with computer servers.

schema.headline: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centres

title: Bank of Ghana: Seven women arrested in Accra over cedi 'money bouquets'
description: Ghanaian authorities have arrested seven people for allegedly using banknotes to make so-called "money bouquets" and decorate cakes.The Bank of Ghana
body: Ghanaian authorities have arrested seven people for allegedly using banknotes to make so-called "money bouquets" and decorate cakes.The Bank of Ghana says the practice is illegal and amounts to misuse and improper handling of the cedi, the national currency.The arrests, carried out in collaboration with the police, followed a tip-off that led to a swoop on the suspects, all women, accused of selling the bouquets in different parts of the capital, Accra.The arrests are the biggest enforcement of the law against misusing the currency. In July, the bank issued a notice warning this could amount to an offence.It warned against "acts that tend to depreciate or impair the national currency, including any conduct that undermines its lawful value or use".Bouquets of banknotes or cakes decorated with currency are often ordered as gifts for weddings, birthdays, graduations and other celebrations.The police have launched investigations, and the authorities say the suspects will be prosecuted. They could face a fine or jail term, to be determined by the court.Dinah Bonzi, an official in the Bank of Ghana's currency department, said anyone aiding or promoting such activities could also be arrested and prosecuted.''The Ghana cedi is legal tender… and must be treated with respect. The misuse or abuse of the currency is an offence and may attract sanctions under the law,'' she said."Today's arrest should serve as a clear warning to the public. Let us all handle the Ghana cedi with dignity."The central bank has repeatedly warned against activities such as "spraying" - or throwing money at events such as weddings - writing on or altering notes and using them in decorations such as floral-like bouquets in weddings, birthdays and other occasions.The use of money decorations has become more common in Ghana in recent years, with the practice also gaining a foothold in other African countries.In recent years authorities in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Botswana have also issued warnings against misusing the national currencies.

schema.headline: Bank of Ghana: Seven women arrested in Accra over cedi 'money bouquets'

title: Nigerian Air Force plane crash: Bola Tinubu declares three days of mourning as 25 killed
description: Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has declared three days of national mourning after a military aircraft crashed in southern Ondo State, killing 25 peop
body: Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has declared three days of national mourning after a military aircraft crashed in southern Ondo State, killing 25 people.Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo on Monday said 32 people had died but on Tuesday the Air Force clarified that 25 people had been killed - five crew and 20 passengers.Authorities say the plane was on a routine mission from Benin City to Lagos when it came down in a swamp near a naval base on Monday morning. After reaching the site, the aircraft was found to be submerged under water, officials said.A resident told the BBC that clothes and shoes had been found at the site. Smoke could be seen rising from the area.It is the deadliest crash involving a Nigerian military aircraft since 1992.The Nigerian Air Force has released the names of those killed, showing that 19 of those on board were military personnel.Tinubu offered his deepest condolences to those killed and has ordered a full investigation.The president also ordered national flags to be flown at half-mast across the country as a mark of respect for those who died."This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation," Tinubu said."Our Air Force personnel put their lives on the line every day to secure Nigeria. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten," he added.The aviation minister earlier said he had been informed "of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today". Keyamo said "efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive" before subsequent confirmation that it had crashed near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo state.He said search and rescue efforts were ongoing.The crashed plane, described as an ATR-42 aircraft, carries between 30 and 50 passengers, according to its manufacturers.

schema.headline: Nigerian Air Force plane crash: Bola Tinubu declares three days of mourning as 25 killed

title: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
description: Belgian-born physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from sp
body: Belgian-born physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space, shedding light on the distant universe.Halzen led the development of IceCube at the South Pole, which uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice fitted with light sensors to detect particles called neutrinos. These carry information about violent, high-energy processes in the cosmos.The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said "his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory".He first presented his vision for detecting neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988.Halzen, who is now a US citizen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, told a news conference that he was surprised his idea worked so well."I have to emphasise how lucky I was. Because when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself."On the rare occasions when a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it produces fast-moving charged particles. It is these racing through the ice, which give off a blue glow, which sensitive light detectors can pick up.The pattern and timing of that light allow scientists to estimate the direction the neutrino came from — helping them trace its origins in the cosmos. But these interactions are so rare that the observatory needed an enormous volume of clear ice.Halzen's idea was to use a vast natural ice sheet in Antarctica. So began an audacious plan to build a neutrino observatory at the geographic South Pole, with thousands of light sensors embedded deep in the ice.The neutrino's ghostly nature, the very thing that makes it so hard to detect, also makes it a powerful messenger from the distant Universe. Neutrinos rarely interact with material in its way, so they can go right through dense regions that light cannot easily penetrate. And because they have no electric charge, magnetic fields do not bend their paths through space. That means their direction of arrival can point scientists back towards their source.Their energies carry further insight into the processes that created them - helping scientists investigate how exploding stars and the environments around giant black holes accelerate particles to extraordinary energies. Louis Barson, director of science at the Institute of Physics in London, said the IceCube Observatory had enabled astronomers to investigate phenomena that conventional telescopes cannot see."The discoveries that have followed are helping us understand some of the most energetic and mysterious processes in the universe - and that's thanks to Professor Halzen's work," he added.Prof Subir Sarkar, physicist from the University of Oxford, quoted the French novelist Marcel Proust in describing his assessment of Halzen's contribution to science:"'The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is'."Francis Halzen has led the IceCube collaboration on just such a voyage of discovery and opened a new window on to our Universe".

schema.headline: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics

title: US military will execute Fort Hood shooter by firing squad, a first in 60 years
description: The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first military execution in more than 60 years.Nidal Hasan fata
body: The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first military execution in more than 60 years.Nidal Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that US defence secretary Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two."Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote on X.Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.Watch: Why is America running out of execution drugs?, externalHasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward. The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.

schema.headline: US military will execute Fort Hood shooter by firing squad, a first in 60 years

title: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
description: Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly wo
body: Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as  "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.Trump, while speaking on Monday in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made. The morning after Trump's statement, Governor Newsom announced that the "dangerous - if not treasonous" statement had prompted him to direct California's State Threat Assessment Center to "monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the remarks as an invitation" to target California.The agency is designed to detect and prevent security threats in the state.San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk". Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders. In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality". "He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money". The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others. "He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added. San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast. It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at. Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US. It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.

schema.headline: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego

title: Nepal floods: Many of those swept away aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" gr
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the deadByAzadeh MoshiriSouth Asia correspondentAt the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month.In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites.With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead.Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati.The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave. "I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says.He has little doubt they are dead. But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leaveSection 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month.Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance.Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death.But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare."In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari.He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues.For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate.When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them.Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed.Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data.The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol.The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over.Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality.Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue."Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC.He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to.For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with griefThe government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households.This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family.The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster.Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied."We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities."The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution.In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required.The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to £3.6bn ($4.8bn).Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Relatives carry Kush grass effigies for cremation during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missingAt the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy. Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects.Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming."When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders.This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster.For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar.He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati.But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village.Once again, he is without a home."I have lost everything," he said.So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal.Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies.He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home.Additional reporting: Rajneesh Bhandari

schema.headline: Nepal floods: Many of those swept away aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo

title: Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
description: Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power,
body: Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant. Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved. Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration". "The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says. "On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years". Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly €400,000 ($450,000; £340,000). His trial is ongoing.

schema.headline: Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason

title: Lionel Messi - Argentina v Benin: The small African nation ready for Messi's big night
description: One of Benin's best-known players is their captain, Steve Mounie.The forward plays for German Bundesliga side FC Augsburg, but will also be known to H
body: One of Benin's best-known players is their captain, Steve Mounie.The forward plays for German Bundesliga side FC Augsburg, but will also be known to Huddersfield Town fans having played for the club between 2017-2020.He's been a regular with the national side for more than a decade but says he's never played a game for them outside of Africa."When the coach called me and told me about this game. We didn't know it was going to be the last game of Leo Messi," Mounie told BBC Sport."It was like the cherry on top of the cake. It adds some more values to this big event for Benin, and it's going to be a big event for the world of football."However, injury means Mounie will play no part in the game. Instead of staying at home recovering, however, he says this was not a moment he could miss out on."I cannot play," he said. "I just came to join the team, to support the team. And, I need to be honest with this because football is my passion. I came for myself."I even paid for my own ticket to come here."I would prefer to be on the bench, but if they tell me that I need to be in the stand, I will be in the stand. There is no problem, but I want to see the game from a pitch view."The former Premier League striker says, while the result of the friendly is largely inconsequential, those players who are selected will know it's a great chance to enhance their reputations and that of Beninese football."We are a team that is very disciplined," said Mounie. "We have a lot of young talent in the team right now that have good technical skills. We are always willing to go forward. We play pressing football, but when we cannot, we stick together and we fight."We are a team like a family, And I think we can relate to this Argentina team because they feel like they are like a family too, which Messi is a father to."Argentina warmed up for the fixture against Benin by defeating fellow west African side Burkina Faso 7-0.Many will be predicting a similar scoreline this game - and it's unlikely Messi will play the full 90 minutes.A more likely scenario is that, with Argentina a few goals to the good, Messi will be substituted in the second half, allowing the sold-out crowd at Estadio Monumental to say farewell to their country's greatest sports star.Once the final whistle does go - don't be surprised if there's a rush towards the World Cup-winning captain."To get hold of a Messi match-worn shirt is incredibly tough because everybody knows how valuable they are," said Doug Bierton, founder of Classic Football Shirts."So every player on the pitch is looking to swap with him. It's the first time a legend has bowed out with a special edition shirt."Bierton, whose private collection of iconic football shirts reaches into the thousands, says the last match-worn Messi shirt would be collector's dream.He ranks it in the same category as Diego Maradona's shirt worn when he scored his 'Hand of God' goal against England at the 1986 World Cup. A jersey which sold for £7.1m in an auction in May 2022.Another item considered in that realm is Zinedine Zidane's shirt from the last time he played for France - which ended in a red card after being sent off for headbutting Italy's Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final.The fact Messi's shirt is being worn in a friendly - yet considered in such high regard - is perhaps testament to the belief he is the greatest footballer ever.So Bierton predicts it won't be just Benin players who will be after the jersey."I'm sure some of his team-mates will be too, he's good friends with [Rodrigo] De Paul," he said. "He'll probably be after it as well. Does he get a gift, a retirement present?"The kit man will be after it. Who knows? I'm literally going to watch the match just to see who he swaps shirts with."

schema.headline: Lionel Messi - Argentina v Benin: The small African nation ready for Messi's big night

title: AfD candidate Rausch elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time
description: A month after Germany's far-right AfD scored a decisive victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the party's candidate Tobias Rausch has been el
body: A month after Germany's far-right AfD scored a decisive victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the party's candidate Tobias Rausch has been elected as parliament speaker there too.Not since World War Two has a far-right party secured the post of speaker, and protesters outside the building in Magdeburg held up banners saying, "Never again is now".Although the AfD fell three seats short of a majority in last month's election, Rausch, 35, comfortably won Tuesday's vote with the support of 9 MPs from other parties."The days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past," Rausch said after the vote, rejecting a post-war consensus in German politics not to work with the far right.This was the first time since last month's state vote that Saxony-Anhalt's newly elected representatives had gathered in parliament, and regional Greens party leader Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said "a line has been crossed" with the election of a far-right speaker of parliament, and it was a watershed moment."We will not let ourselves be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights are curtailed either here or for people in the state," she said.The AfD is considered pro-Russian and anti-immigrant, with plans to segregate child refugees in schools, as well as intolerant towards the LGBT community. Within Saxony-Anhalt it is also classed as "right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence, a description rejected by party leaders. Until now its members have sat on the right fringe of the state parliament, but ahead of Tuesday's inaugural session it successfully argued that it should now sit in the centre.

schema.headline: AfD candidate Rausch elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time

title: Gyanesh Kumar: Police detain opposition leaders in Delhi demanding election commission chief's resignation
description: "Some of the MPs tried to take some other roads to the Election Commission building. We have officers stationed at multiple points, from where the pro
body: "Some of the MPs tried to take some other roads to the Election Commission building. We have officers stationed at multiple points, from where the protesters were picked up in buses and taken to different police stations," Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Manjeet Sheoran told the BBC. The police did not disclose how many lawmakers had been detained. The opposition said 237 MPs from a range of parties participated in the march.Tuesday's protest came just four days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a Gen Z-backed online satirical movement, organised demonstrations in Mumbai and Delhi, also demanding the CEC's resignation. The group has described those demonstrations as the beginning of a nationwide campaign and has called for another round of protests on 10 October.At the centre of the controversy is the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The exercise began in the eastern state of Bihar in June 2025 before being expanded to other parts of the country. The Election Commission says the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters from electoral rolls. More than 130 million names have so far been removed from draft voter lists nationwide.Opposition parties and activists allege that many eligible voters have been wrongly excluded and accuse the poll body of conducting the process improperly.The campaign against Kumar gathered momentum after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions and orders they said had been issued in the Election Commission's name without their knowledge.According to the report, the objections related to issues including additions and deletions from voter rolls, access to the voter database and the security of electoral data. Some concerns were linked directly to the electoral roll revision programme.The Election Commission, a three-member body comprising the chief election commissioner and two election commissioners, defended its decision-making process, saying differing views were part of institutional functioning and that decisions had ultimately been taken unanimously.The revelations nevertheless triggered a political backlash, with opposition leaders intensifying calls for Kumar's resignation.Security was tightened around the Election Commission headquarters on Tuesday, with police barricading roads along the route between parliament and the commission's office.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge described three demands as "non-negotiable": Kumar's resignation, cancellation of the SIR exercise and a return to paper ballot voting.Mocking the election chief, Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India's lower house of parliament, tweeted: "Gyanesh, it's done, bro. Time to resign."The BJP condemned the protests.BJP MP Sambit Patra described them as a "sponsored attempt" to bring about a change of power through "anarchy". He accused opposition parties of seeking to undermine constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission.The controversy has also reached India's Supreme Court, which has asked both the federal government and the Election Commission to respond to a petition alleging that Kumar took key decisions without the approval of the two other election commissioners.The petition argues that Kumar exercised powers that belong to the commission collectively and seeks a ruling that any such actions were unauthorised.The court indicated that Election Commission decisions must be taken either unanimously or by majority vote and suggested that decisions could be set aside if found to have bypassed that process. However, it declined to suspend Kumar at this stage, saying it would first hear the Election Commission's response and examine relevant records.The BBC has contacted the Election Commission for comment on Tuesday's protest.

schema.headline: Gyanesh Kumar: Police detain opposition leaders in Delhi demanding election commission chief's resignation

title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
description: OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had ad
body: OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox."We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake."In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said."The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents."Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations"."We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI."We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.  An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard."In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association. Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

schema.headline: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'

title: A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
description: A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have foun
body: A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found.The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas.But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals.Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird.One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley."These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas.Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas."If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan.The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation.While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity."There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said.The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'Why the mighty Himalayas are getting harder and harder to seeAccording to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios.Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats.The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit."These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption.The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says.The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar.They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023.Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said.The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear."This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall.Bird calls are one of the most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication in the natural world, and significant changes can interfere with, among other things, their mating success."When a species must raise its pitch to be heard over tourist traffic, or climb higher as meadows turn crowded, it reveals how human pressure is rewriting the rules of life in the Himalaya," says Anjal Prakash, a public policy professor at FLAME University and contributor to IPCC reports.Lochan says he and his team consider this a preliminary study and hope to expand the scope and depth of it.The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences, and more research is needed. But together, the two studies signal broader ecological stress across the Himalayas."In listening to the monal, we hear the Himalayas asking for space, silence and care," says Prakash.

schema.headline: A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows

title: Ship sinks and crew missing after Black Sea drone attack
description: A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.A second vessel - carr
body: A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued. Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine. Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable".Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania.It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board.A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched. Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain. Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning."Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning.""Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.

schema.headline: Ship sinks and crew missing after Black Sea drone attack
